entries.section: 1. The Lord goes out to judgment:

paragraphs.text: 1 The word of the LORD that came to Micah the Morasthite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. 2 Hear, all ye people; hearken, O earth, and all that therein is: and let the Lord GOD be witness against you, the Lord from his holy temple. 3 For, behold, the LORD cometh forth out of his place, and will come down, and tread upon the high places of the earth. 4 And the mountains shall be molten under him, and the valleys shall be cleft, as wax before the fire, and as the waters that are poured down a steep place.
The word of the LORD that came to Micah the Morasthite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. [1]

"The word of the Lord," or "the word of Yahweh": the prophet affirms that what he utters and what he writes is not from himself, but is the message of Yahweh, carrying divine authority. Yahweh directed this message to His prophet Micah so that he might proclaim it to the people as well as to the leaders.

The name of the prophet, like that of other prophets such as Hosea, Joel and Obadiah, reveals his message. The word "Micah," as we have seen, means "none is like Yahweh," although St. Ambrose sees that its meaning is "one with God." It is as though the prophet is challenging the false prophets and the stubborn, wicked and resisting ones, that there is none like Yahweh, and that He cannot be resisted!

St. Jerome sees that the word "Moresheth" in Hebrew means "my possessions," and for this reason he sees in Micah one who possesses Christ or who is an heir with Him. If the Book of Micah began with the public trial brought by God Himself, then in His case, even when He chastens, He does not take vengeance, but desires to qualify us for the eternal inheritance and heavenly glory.

* "Micah: its meaning is "one with God," or, as we find in another place, "one is the son of the Morasthite," that is, "the son of the heir." Who is the Heir but the Son of God, who says: "All things are delivered unto me of my Father" (Mt 11:27)? He who is the Heir desires us to be partakers in the inheritance.

You ask well: Who is Micah? He is not of the people, but he was chosen to receive the grace of God, and the Holy Spirit speaks through him. He began his prophecy in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. But this order in the presentation of the vision to him has its meaning, for it begins with the age of wicked kings and ends with a good king.

St. Ambrose As for his saying "which he saw," it does not mean a bodily sight, but a spiritual vision by the mind, for the Spirit of the Lord opened the eyes of Micah to perceive the message which he is bound to witness to and proclaim to the people.

Micah prophesied in the age of Ahaz, who is considered one of the worst kings of Judah, and he also prophesied in the age of Hezekiah, the godly man of reform. In the age of Ahaz he did not fear to speak of God's chastenings of Judah, but he opened the door of consolations for the holy souls returning to the Lord. And in the reign of the godly Hezekiah he spoke of the necessity of inner spiritual reform. Thus, with the changing circumstances of the times, the word of God remains firm: it does not flatter the wicked, nor does it close the door of hope before them, nor does it delight in outward reforms without entering into the depths.
Hear, all ye people.
Hearken, O earth, and all that therein is.

entries.section: 1. The Lord goes out to judgment:

paragraphs.text: And let the Lord GOD be witness against you, the Lord from his holy temple. [2]

Since many of the people of God stopped their ears from listening to the voice of the Lord, He extended the call to the earth that it might open its ears and listen to Him. As the Lord Christ said: "That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven" (Mt 8:11).

God, who loves His heavenly and earthly creation, often summons them to listen to His word (Isa 1:2; Deut 32:1); He asks them to listen to Him with attentive ears, even when He judges His people, for He desires to reveal to all the secrets of His dealings with His creation. There is no partiality with God: if His people sin, He calls the Gentiles to attend their trial, that it may be a practical lesson for their acceptance of the faith.

He is the Lord of all creation and its Master; He speaks from His holy temple, that is, from heaven, which is consecrated to Him as the Holy One. From there He speaks, longing that all creation be sanctified and become a living icon of the Holy One. Whether He chastens or shows tenderness, the aim of the Holy One is the holiness of His creation.

* "For this is the will of God, even your sanctification" (1 Thess 4:3)... Notice how he does not look to any subject with such zeal as this. For he writes of it in another place: "Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord" (Heb 12:14). Why should we marvel if he writes to his disciples about this matter everywhere? In his epistle to Timothy he says: "keep thyself pure" (1 Tim 5:22), and in his second epistle to the Corinthians he says: "In much patience, in fastings, in pureness" (2 Cor 6:5-6).

St. John Chrysostom Since the rational people became corrupt and acted irrationally against their Creator, the Creator wished to rebuke them through irrational nature; so He often summoned the lifeless earth and the heaven with its stars, by the mouth of the prophets, to witness His judgment of His people. So it is no wonder that the earth moved and quaked when the hand of the creature was stretched out to crucify the incarnate divine Word, and that the sun withheld its rays to reprove the ungrateful crucifiers and bear witness against them with darkness.
The creation which God brought into being to serve man became a witness against him and a reprover of him for his disobedience and corruption.

entries.section: 1. The Lord goes out to judgment:

paragraphs.text: For, behold, the LORD cometh forth out of his place, and will come down, and tread upon the high places of the earth. [3]

God used to go out to His people so that He might bring them out to Himself, and to come down to them in His love so as to lift them up into His embrace. Now, since they persisted in corruption in stubbornness, He went out to judge them and chasten them.

The prophet portrays God as coming down from heaven, walking upon the mountains, to shatter Samaria for its insistence on the worship of idols and its practice of abominations; and its corruption had crept into Judah, so that the judgment of Judah too was at the doors.

The Lord's coming down and treading upon the high places of the earth points to two things. First, that the Word of God, the Creator and Savior, goes forth as though from His place, for He says of His incarnation and becoming man: "for I proceeded forth and came from God" (Jn 8:42); and second, that the Lord sits upon the throne of His mercy, and when He chastens firmly He appears as one who goes out of His place to shatter the pride and loftiness of man. As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: "For, behold, the LORD cometh out of his place to punish" (Isa 26:21). He is a heavenly Father who longs not to punish; if He chastens, it is as one who has gone out of His place, that is, out of mercy full of tenderness and compassion. Our iniquity and disobedience make Him as one who goes out of His place to punish... Even in His going out He seeks to gather us to Himself, to bring us back to the throne of His mercy.
Some see that He is pointing here to the Lord's going out as upon the clouds to judge the wicked who exalt themselves, and to glorify His humble believers.

* Let us now consider the statement of Jesus: "for I proceeded forth and came from God" (Jn 8:42). It seems useful to me to set beside these words the following words from Micah: "Hear, O my people, my words, and let the earth and all that therein is hearken, and let the Lord be a witness in the midst of you, the Lord from the holy house. For, behold, the LORD cometh forth out of his place, and treadeth upon the high places of the earth, and the mountains shall be moved under him, and the valleys shall melt as wax before the fire, and as the waters that are poured down a steep place" (Mic 1:2-4). Now consider whether the statement "I proceeded forth from God" is equivalent to this statement; since the Son is in the Father, being in the form of the Father before He emptied Himself (Phil 2:6-7), He was God in His place, so it appears as though contradictory that He goes forth from the Father and at the same time is still in God.

* It is said that God comes down when He condescends to give attention to human weakness. This must be discerned especially in the case of our Lord and Savior, who, since He "thought it not robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, and took upon him the form of a servant" (Phil 2:6-7), in this way came down. For "no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man which is in heaven" (Jn 3:13). For the Lord came down, not only to care for us but also to bear what is ours, since He "took upon him the form of a servant"; and though He Himself is invisible by nature, being equal with the Father, yet He took a visible form, since He "was found in fashion as a man" (Phil 2:7).
Origen And the mountains shall be molten under him, and the valleys shall be cleft, as wax before the fire.

entries.section: 1. The Lord goes out to judgment:

paragraphs.text: And as the waters that are poured down a steep place. [4]

When the Lord goes out to judge His people, the mountains and the high places used for the worship of idols cannot stand before Him, those which represent impregnable fortresses to protect them from any foreign invasion; for the Lord treads upon them, and they melt and become dust. Nor can the valleys support them, for they melt before Him like wax before the fire. Neither the great men, who reckon themselves lofty mountains, nor those of the lower classes, who are like the valleys, can defend the wicked people before God.

It is related in the Coptic (Bohairic) Life of St. Pachomius: [On another occasion, as (his disciple Theodore) was sitting by himself in a place reading the book of the Twelve Prophets, he came to the prophet Micah. An angel of the Lord appeared to him and asked him about this verse from Micah: "as the waters that are poured down a steep place." He said to him: "What do you think is the meaning of this?" And as he was perplexed about it, trying to understand, the angel answered him: "Theodore, why have you not grasped its meaning? Is it not clear that it is the water of the river that flows down from Paradise?" And when the angel had said this, he no longer saw him].
* Like wax, which cannot bear to approach the fire, and like water flowing down, so will all the wicked be when the Lord comes, for they dissolve and vanish.
St. Jerome

5 For the transgression of Jacob is all this, and for the sins of the house of Israel. What is the transgression of Jacob? is it not Samaria? and what are the high places of Judah? are they not Jerusalem? 6 "Therefore I will make Samaria as an heap of the field, and as plantings of a vineyard: and I will pour down the stones thereof into the valley, and I will discover the foundations thereof. 7 And all the graven images thereof shall be beaten to pieces, and all the hires thereof shall be burned with the fire, and all the idols thereof will I lay desolate: for she gathered it of the hire of an harlot, and they shall return to the hire of an harlot."
For the transgression of Jacob is all this, and for the sins of the house of Israel.
What is the transgression of Jacob? is it not Samaria?
And what are the high places of Judah? are they not Jerusalem? [5]

He began with Samaria, the capital of Israel, as the center of the worship of Baal, from which idolatrous worship seeped into Judah. Then he spoke of the high places of Judah, where idolatrous worship crept in. Samaria was punished first at the hand of Assyria, and afterward Jerusalem, the capital of Judah, at the hand of Babylon.
By the high places here he points to the worship of idols that was carried on there, which the Law forbade (Deut 13).
Sadly, the focus of sin in the two kingdoms was the two capitals: Samaria and Jerusalem.
Therefore I will make Samaria as an heap of the field, and as plantings of a vineyard: and I will pour down the stones thereof into the valley, and I will discover the foundations thereof. [6]

Here he presents a terrifying judgment as the natural fruit of the iniquity of Samaria. Samaria was turned into a ruin because of continual wars (Isa 21:1-3). God allows Samaria to be shattered and its stones to be poured down into the valley, so that its foundations are completely laid bare. To this day Samaria is heaps of stones, not only on the hill, but even in the fields below, and archaeologists have uncovered the foundations of the palaces of Omri and Ahab.

Samaria, which prided itself on its wealth and the multitude of its inhabitants, becomes heaps of refuse of vineyards and fields and of stones. They were gathered together to be cast out. Perhaps he began with the plantings of vineyards and afterward the heaps of stones, because Samaria was originally vineyard fields before it was built up as a capital, as though it returns to what it was, and even to something worse, for the buildings collapse and are turned into heaps of stones, losing their nature as a royal capital to become a ruin.

And all the graven images thereof shall be beaten to pieces, and all the hires thereof shall be burned with the fire, and all the idols thereof will I lay desolate: for she gathered it of the hire of an harlot, and they shall return to the hire of an harlot. [7]

The prophet looked at the civilization that Samaria had attained, which came only through idol worship, as well as from the hire of harlots; so it is fitting that its graven images be beaten to pieces, because they were made from the hire of harlots.

Many harlots used to offer from the hire of harlotry to the pagan temples, to be spent on them and for their adornment; so when these temples collapse with their abominations, it is as though they returned what they had received to the harlots.

8 Therefore I will wail and howl, I will go stripped and naked: I will make a wailing like the dragons, and mourning as the owls. 9 For her wound is incurable; for it is come unto Judah; he is come unto the gate of my people, even to Jerusalem.

Danger threatens Jerusalem, for the Assyrian army sweeps over the coastal plain in the direction of Egypt, bursting into the place where Micah dwelt, crossing from one city to another, and reaching the walls of Jerusalem. The prophet Isaiah described the same situation while dwelling inside the city (Isa 10:28-34), whereas Micah described it from outside the city, at a distance of about 20 miles.
Therefore I will wail and howl.
I will go stripped and naked.
I will make a wailing like the dragons. [8]
As the prophet laments for Israel, he does not cease weeping and crying out until his voice becomes like the voice of the jackals, and like the voice of the young of the female ostrich.

Captives used to be led barefoot and naked; so the soul of the prophet was embittered, and he became like a captive of grief, losing his garments and his sandals, to walk in the road barefoot and naked.

Earlier, the prophet Isaiah had walked barefoot and naked for three years at the command of the Lord, as a sign and wonder upon Egypt and Ethiopia (Cush), a prophecy of their captivity at the hand of Assyria (Isa 20:2-4).

* Isaiah's walking naked without shame was a symbol of the coming captivity. Jeremiah was sent from Jerusalem to the Euphrates, and left his girdle to rot in the camp of the Chaldeans among the Assyrians, the enemies of his people (Jer 13:6-7)... He urges men to repent.

St. Jerome * The captivity of our brothers must be reckoned as though it were our own captivity. The sorrows of those in danger are our sorrows. You must be sure that there is one body of our unity. It is not our love alone but also our religion that moves and encourages us to rescue the members of our family.

St. Cyprian Whoever looks at the prophet Micah, weeping and lamenting, walking stripped of his outer garment, barefoot, makes light of him as a naked and barefoot peasant. But heaven looks at him and sees in his tears, his cries, his nakedness and his bare feet the image of wonderful love, which sees its people about 150 years later in captivity, and so reckons itself a captive with them and shares with them the bitterness of their souls. As St. Paul says: "Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body" (Heb 13:3). And his saying: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is offended, and I burn not?" (2 Cor 11:29).
For her wound is incurable, and mourning as the owls.
For it is come unto Judah; he is come unto the gate of my people, even to Jerusalem. [9]
The corruption of Samaria and its worship of idols spread in Israel, and crept into Judah, until it reached the gates of Jerusalem, and she shared with it its evil.
The wounds became incurable, on the spiritual, social and political levels; this is what befell Jerusalem.

The "gate of the city" in the East referred to the men of state who worked with the king and to his counselors; they used to gather at the gate of the city. This continued even in the days of the Turks, for the Turkish Sultan with his entourage was called "the Sublime Porte." Sublime Porte.

10 Declare ye it not at Gath, weep ye not at all: in the house of Aphrah roll thyself in the dust. 11 Pass ye away, thou inhabitant of Saphir, having thy shame naked: the inhabitant of Zaanan came not forth in the mourning of Beth-ezel; he shall receive of you his standing. 12 For the inhabitant of Maroth waited carefully for good: but evil came down from the LORD unto the gate of Jerusalem. 13 O thou inhabitant of Lachish, bind the chariot to the swift beast: she is the beginning of the sin to the daughter of Zion: for the transgressions of Israel were found in thee. 14 Therefore shalt thou give presents to Moresheth-gath: the houses of Achzib shall be a lie to the kings of Israel. 15 Yet will I bring an heir unto thee, O inhabitant of Mareshah: he shall come unto Adullam the glory of Israel. 16 Make thee bald, and poll thee for thy delicate children; enlarge thy baldness as the eagle; for they are gone into captivity from thee.

The prophet Micah points to ten cities, the first five north of Jerusalem, and the last southwest of Jerusalem or south of it. It is as though destruction will come not upon Jerusalem alone, but upon the cities surrounding it also. All these cities are pagan. Destruction will come upon all, so long as they insist on their evil.

Some scholars see that some of them bear symbolic names, which reveal the role of sin and its hideousness in the life of the community, as in the life of the person determined on his evil. 1. A stumbling block: the prophet asks the inhabitants of Jerusalem, when captivity comes upon them after a century and a half, not to tell the pagan cities of Philistia, such as Gath and Acco (Acre), what has befallen them [10], and not to weep before their inhabitants, for they have become a stumbling block to them. Moreover, the word "Acco" is derived from the Hebrew word that means weeping. 2. Return to dust: instead of the heaven prepared for the believer, the person determined on his evil wallows in the dust, and hears the divine voice: "Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return," and so he becomes Aphrah (dust) [10].

* There is nothing that weighs down the soul and presses upon it and brings it down below like the sense of sin, and there is nothing that gives it wings and lifts it to the heights like the attainment of righteousness and virtue.

St. John Chrysostom 3. The stripping of the garment of righteousness: if the word "Shaphir" means beauty, then sin strips man of the garment of righteousness, and Shaphir becomes naked and ashamed [11] instead of the inner beauty of the soul. 4. A sudden distress: the word "Zaanan" means "city of the flock." As the people are surprised, like a flock of sheep, by the calamity that comes upon them as the fruit of their sins, from the horror of the surprise they do not go out of the city, but all walk around one another, and everyone stumbles. Perhaps this happens because the calamity falls upon the whole community. 5. A general calamity: the word "Beth-ezel" means "a nearby place." So everyone stands in his place, and there is none who goes out to his near neighbor to seek his help, since the calamity falls upon all. 6. Bitterness of soul: the word "Maroth" means "bitter." The wicked person may think that he enjoys good things and pleasures by practicing evil and sin, but soon he loses his good things and his life is turned into an unbearable bitterness. 7. The demolition of fortresses and the loss of security: Lachish was one of the most fortified cities of Judah, thinking that the enemy would not be able to storm it. But the prophet Micah sees with the eye of prophecy Sennacherib besieging it, and sees its storming (Isa 36:1-2). Its men try to flee with their chariots and horses, but to where? They were driven into captivity.
* As those who come out of earthly prisons are brought bound in their chains to the place of trial, so all souls bound with the chains of their various sins are led to the dreadful judgment seat.

* When you see the rich man entangled in his countless affairs, do not reckon him rich, but in this he is wretched. For he is in these chains under the authority of a harsh jailer: the evil love of riches. Because of this he is not permitted to depart from the prison, but is bound with thousands of chains and guards and doors and bolts (locks), and when he is cast into the inner prison it tracks him down so that he may feel pleasure in these chains, so that he finds no hope of deliverance from the evils that press upon him.

St. John Chrysostom 8. There is no salvation by mere human wisdom: even the prophet's own city, Moresheth-gath, gives gifts to flatter the Philistines into helping it, but to no avail. 9. Lies and deception: the word "Achzib" means "a lie" or "deception," for the people were deceived by the false prophets, and thought that they were in peace and security, but we shall uncover their deception after it is too late. She becomes an inheritance for the enemy; Achzib is joined with Mareshah, but discovers her inability to help, since Mareshah herself becomes an inheritance for the enemy. 10. The loss of glory: the great and the nobles flee to Adullam, famous for its caves. They try to hide in the caves, and so the glory of Judah becomes imprisoned in them. 11. Unceasing mourning: it was among the ancient customs to cut the hair, especially for girls and women, at the death of someone dear to them, and when they are carried away into captivity. So baldness here points to the lack of consolation, like one who has lost his dearest or been led away as a captive.
Declare ye it not at Gath, weep ye not at all.
In the house of Aphrah roll thyself in the dust. [10]
Rolling in the dust points to intense grief.

Aphrah is a Hebrew name meaning "dust." Beth Aphrah lies on the slope of the mountains of Judah, and its location is not known precisely; J. Simons sees that it is the Wadi el-Afr between ed-Dawaimeh and Tell ed-Duweir. Some see that it is et-Taiyibeh between Hebron and Beit Jibrin.
Pass ye away, thou inhabitant of Saphir, having thy shame naked.
The inhabitant of Zaanan came not forth.
In the mourning of Beth-ezel; he shall receive of you his standing. [11]

Shaphir: Shaphir, Saphir, a Hebrew name meaning "beautiful," a city in Judah; some see that it is now Tell es-Suwafir, which lies three and a half miles southeast of Ashdod, and others consider it more likely to be "Khirbet el-Kom" (Kherbet el-Kom) west of Hebron, which lies in the "Wadi es-Saffar," in which the echo of the ancient name is heard.

He likens these cities to a woman who loses every possibility of covering herself, and so walks among men naked and ashamed. She is led as a captive in great disgrace, and no man can move to rescue her from the violent enemy.

* Would that we rid ourselves of the filth of sin, so that the original beauty of virtue may appear. David the prophet says in the Psalm: "O Lord, by Your beauty You gave strength to my beauty" (Ps 29:8). Let us be purified so that the image of God may appear in us, and this is what God wants from us, that we be without spot, without lack and without blemish.
St. Dorotheus Zaanan: some see that the prophet is playing on the word to give a symbolic meaning.
The inhabitant of Zaanan does not go out of her house, but lurks in terror awaiting her bitter fate, when the invader attacks her and takes her captive.

The city of Beth-ezel: a Hebrew name meaning "the nearby place" or "the house of separation." It is said to be "Asil," or Deir el-Asal, southwest of Hebron and about two miles east of Tell Beit Mirsim. It was most likely fortified and would resist the invader, but its people weep for what has befallen their brothers in the other cities, and grow weary from much lamenting.
For the inhabitant of Maroth waited carefully for good: but evil came down from the LORD unto the gate of Jerusalem. [12]

Maroth: it lies in western Judah, and was perhaps the same as "Maarath." Some see that this name is a play on the word "Maarath" (Josh 15:59) to give the meaning of bitterness, and that it is now called Beit Ummar.
* The things of grace are accompanied by joy, peace, love and truth... But the forms of sin are accompanied by disturbance, and neither love nor joy toward God.

St. Macarius the Great * What if a man is rich, and of the nobility? When some sin takes him captive, he becomes more corrupt than any corruption. If a man who is a king has been taken captive by barbarians, he becomes the most wretched of men; so it is with sin, for it is barbarian, and the soul that becomes a captive does not know how to free itself from captivity, and sin plays the role of a tyrant to destroy everyone who clings to it.
St. John Chrysostom O thou inhabitant of Lachish, bind the chariot to the swift beast.
She is the beginning of the sin to the daughter of Zion: for the transgressions of Israel were found in thee. [13]

Lachish: a fortified city lying in the plains of Judah (Josh 15:33, 39). It was known as Tell el-Hesi, which is about 16 miles northeast of Gaza and eleven miles northeast of Gaza and 11 southwest of Beit Jibrin.
The inhabitant of Lachish is told to flee from the coming invasion, because she was the first to drive Zion to commit sin.
Therefore shalt thou give presents to Moresheth-gath.
The houses of Achzib shall be a lie to the kings of Israel. [14]

"Beth Achzib" (Achzib) means "the house of deception," for it deceived the kings of Israel. It was also called Chezib (Gen 38:5), and Cozeba (1 Chr 4:22). Perhaps the city took this name from a spring in it which flowed in winter and dried up in summer. Some think that it is "Ain Kezbeh" in the Wadi el-Ilah (Valley of Elah) north of Adullam. Others say it is "Tell el-Beida" (Tell el-Beida) southwest of Adullam.
Instead of this city acting against the invaders, it will be helpless and powerless, and perhaps it will turn into a treacherous deceiver on behalf of the invader.
Yet will I bring an heir unto thee, O inhabitant of Mareshah.
He shall come unto Adullam the glory of Israel. [15]

Adullam: a Hebrew name meaning a refuge, mentioned between the towns of Jarmuth and Socoh; it is Canaanite in origin. The Canaanites dwelt in it from the days of Jacob (Gen 38:1-2). Joshua struck it, then Rehoboam fortified it (2 Chr 11:7). The Jews settled in it after the return from the captivity (Neh 11:30). Its site is Tell Sheikh Madhkur. Adullam was surrounded by rugged terrain and was famous for its caves in which men used to hide from the face of war. In it was the cave in which David hid and which he made his headquarters (1 Sam 22:1; 2 Sam 23:13; 1 Chr 11:15), and it is said that it is the cave of the Wadi Khureitun, also called the caves of Id el-Ma, about thirteen miles southwest of Bethlehem, between Lachish and Jerusalem.

Mareshah loses her honor, and the glory stops at Adullam. The prophet Micah warns them of the attack of the enemies, so that the nobles and great men of Judah are forced to flee to these caves to hide, as though the glory of Israel had been buried in these caves.
Make thee bald, and poll thee for thy delicate children.
Enlarge thy baldness as the eagle; for they are gone into captivity from thee. [16]

The prophet portrays the terrible sorrow that comes upon fathers and mothers as they see their sons and daughters taken into captivity. This happened many times, to Israel and to Judah alike, and reached its most terrible form in the final invasion of Israel by Assyria in 722 A.D., which the prophet Micah lived to see, and the final invasion of Judah in 586 B.C.

Israel is like a mother weeping for her cities as for daughters who have died and lost life, and so she declares her grief over them and over her sons who were born in honor and now are led into captivity.
Here Micah speaks of what will come to pass as one who sees it happening while he prophesies concerning them.

* This happened, as we know, since we were told beforehand concerning Judah by the prophet: "enlarge thy baldness as the eagle" (Mic 1:16); for baldness comes upon a man in his head only, but in the case of the eagle it comes upon its whole body. For when it grows very old it sheds the pinion feathers of its wings from its whole body. He (Judah) loses his feathers when he loses his people. He sheds the pinions of his wings with which he was accustomed to fly toward the prey, since all the strong men perish by whom he (Judah) swoops down upon others.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
The bitterness of sin in my mouth!
* I confess to You, O my God:
I drink sin like water, and think there is life and happiness in pleasure!
Reveal to me the bitterness of sin.
Your fiery Spirit exposes my depths, so that I cling to You, O Forgiver of sin!
* You desire to judge me, not to take vengeance on me, but to chasten me in Your mercy, and to qualify me for Your eternal inheritance!
Your fatherhood, even in its firmness, is full of tenderness!
Your care is surpassing; You carry me on Your shoulders!
* Come out to me, and shatter every lofty mountain in my depths, and let all despair in my heart dissolve, and let my sin be dispersed like waters down a steep place!
Shatter my evils, and remove all corruption within me!
* As You come out to me in love, grant me to go out to my brothers!
Let me wail for a wandering soul, and howl for every lost person; how can my heart not burn for every one who stumbles?
How can I not be weak with every weak one?
How can I not count myself a captive with everyone who is captive to sin?
* I return, and my soul groans over my sins and the sins of my brothers!
I confess to You that we have caused many to stumble; let Your grace work in us, that we may glorify You for Your divine work in us!
* Our sin turned us to dust; Your grace lifts us to heaven!
* Our sin made us lose the garment of Your righteousness; Your fiery Spirit restores to us Your righteousness within us!
* Our sin robbed us of our inner peace; Your presence in us grants us Your surpassing peace!
* Our sin embittered our souls; our fellowship with You is sweetness itself!
* Our sin shattered our spiritual walls; Your indwelling is the fiery wall of our souls!
* Our sin deceived us with lies and vain promises.
Your coming down to us lifted us to Your eternal glories!
* Our sin led us into captivity; Your grace grants us the freedom of the glory of the children of God!

1 Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds! when the morning is light, they practise it, because it is in the power of their hand. 2 And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage. 3 Therefore thus saith the LORD; "Behold, against this family do I devise an evil, from which ye shall not remove your necks; neither shall ye go haughtily: for this time is evil.
Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds!
When the morning is light, they practise it, because it is in the power of their hand. [1]

He pronounces woe upon those who stay awake at night planning, in selfishness, to seize what belongs to others, and when the morning comes they carry out what they had planned, because they are men of authority. All that occupies their thoughts and hearts is the coveting of what belongs to others, justifying this to themselves in one way or another. For example, a man reckons that he is more capable of managing and running the field, or that the owner of the field is unable to pay the debt whose interest has accumulated against him and swollen. With consummate skill they conspire how to fulfill the desire of their hearts. If injustice, seizure and covetousness are grave sins, they are graver still when a man devotes himself to arranging them, using his craftiness, his deceit, his resources and his authority! He thinks that no one has the right to call him to account.

It grieves the heart that wicked oppressors devote the night to planning evil and rise early with the light of morning to carry out what they have devised, while we are not occupied at night with prayer and meditation on the word of God, and do not rise early to work for the sake of the Kingdom of God. Therefore the wise man counsels us: "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest" (Eccl 9:10).

What a man thinks about when he lies down for bodily rest reveals what is in his heart, his mind and his intentions. The spiritual man, when he lies down, has his soul lifted up to meditate on the joyful things of God, while the wicked man's soul is immersed in the evils that capture and enslave it. Moreover, just as the night reveals to us what we are by day, so what we think about by night leads to its being done by day, sooner or later. The holiness of our life by day gives us holy thoughts and dreams at night worthy of the children of God, and the holiness of our waking daydreams drives us still more toward spiritual growth in the Lord.
And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage. [2]

King Ahab was a wicked example of exploiting his authority according to the counsel of his wicked wife Jezebel (1 Kgs 21:1-15), when he took possession of the field of Naboth the Jezreelite after contriving his murder. This kind of corruption spread in Judah, and the nobles who held authority were struck with this grave disease.

* O rich man, why do you exalt yourself with your wealth and boast of the glories of your forefathers? Do you take pride in your homeland, and delight in the beauty of your body, and rejoice in a passing honor? Take heed to yourself. Remember that you are a mortal man, and that you are dust and to dust you shall return (Gen 3:19)... Bend down and look at the tombs: can you tell the bones of the poor from the bones of the rich? The bones of slaves from the bones of masters? Be mindful of yourself, then, and give up pride, miserliness and hardness of heart.

* You have become, O wealthy man, a servant of the all-merciful God and His steward before your brothers in servitude. So beware of thinking that these good things are for your belly. Reckon what is in your hands as something foreign to you. These goods charm you for a while, then soon evaporate and vanish, but you will give a strict account of them.

St. Basil the Great They seize the fields of others not only by craftiness and deceit, but by violence and tyranny, usurping the rights of others, against the law. They oppress the master of the house with no regard for his family or his inheritance from his forefathers.
Therefore thus saith the LORD:
Behold, against this family do I devise an evil, from which ye shall not remove your necks; neither shall ye go haughtily: for this time is evil. [3]
By the family he means here the whole kingdom, and by the evil he means here the chastening by captivity, which they see as an evil that has come upon them.

Yahweh repays these oppressors according to their deeds, and allows them the bonds of captivity from which their necks do not escape. Instead of their haughtiness their necks are encircled with fetters, and they are dragged to the land of captivity. Since the rich and the leaders placed a heavy yoke on the class of the peasants, He allows the heavy yoke of captivity to come upon them, and they cannot remove it from their necks; in this He breaks their pride and haughtiness.

4 "In that day shall one take up a parable against you, and lament with a doleful lamentation, and say, We be utterly spoiled: he hath changed the portion of my people: how hath he removed it from me! turning away he hath divided our fields. 5 Therefore thou shalt have none that shall cast a cord by lot in the congregation of the LORD.
In that day shall one take up a parable against you, and lament with a doleful lamentation, and say:
We be utterly spoiled.
He hath changed the portion of my people: how hath he removed it from me!
Turning away he hath divided our fields. [4]

As they plunder the possessions of others, they lose even their own possessions; the enemy takes over the fields, and seizes their lands and their harvests, so that they lose prosperity as well as the lands of their inheritance. They are torn away from them unexpectedly, and they are stunned because of the element of surprise and violence.
When the day of severe chastening comes, their joys are turned into laments, and their laughter into crying out, and they become a byword among their friends and neighbors.

* Thus this wretched soul is shaken (by covetousness), and the dragon of covetousness coils around it, and it cannot free itself, while it strives hard to multiply the heap of money which it has acquired by unlawful means and hateful diligence, accompanied by calamities that do not lessen the intensity of this soul's covetousness but increase its burning, and blind it to everything except running after gain and obtaining money... and stripping itself of faith, whenever it finds a glimmer of hope of obtaining money.

And for this reason he will not scruple to commit the crime of lying, or false witness, or theft, or breaking a promise, or giving way to wounding fits of rage. Also, if he loses hope of obtaining gain, he will not scruple to overstep the limits of propriety and humility, and in all this gold and the love of base profit become a god to him, like those who worship their bellies. For this reason the blessed Apostle, looking at the deadly poison of this plague, did not say only that it is the root of all evils, but also called it "idolatry," saying: "and covetousness, which is idolatry" (Col 3:5).

You see, then, the measure of the fall to which this madness leads step by step, so that the Apostle cries out loudly that it is the worship of false idols, because, overstepping the image and likeness of God (which every one who worships God in spirit and truth must keep in the depths of his soul without falsification), he has preferred to love and cling to the images engraved on gold instead of God.

By such great steps, going downward, he is driven from bad to worse, and finally he does not care to keep for himself, not the virtues of humility, love and obedience, nor even their shadow, besides becoming dissatisfied with everything, grumbling and complaining about every work. Then, having cast all reverence to the winds, like a runaway horse he rushes headlong with loosened reins.

* Do you wish to know how dangerous this temptation is, and its harm to its owner, unless it is uprooted with care, and the destruction it brings upon him, and the various branches of sins that spring from it? Look at Judas, who was numbered among the disciples, and consider how, because he did not move to crush the head of this deadly dragon, he was destroyed by its poison, and how, when he fell into the snare of this lust, it cast him into sin and into a swift fall, so that it seduced him to sell the Redeemer of mankind and the Author of man's salvation for thirty pieces of silver; and that it was not possible to drive him to this wicked sin, the sin of betraying his Master, unless he had been stained by the sin of covetousness. Nor would he have been driven to commit crime against his Master in such a hideous way unless he had accustomed himself to steal from the purse entrusted to him.
St. John Cassian Therefore thou shalt have none that shall cast a cord by lot in the congregation of the LORD. [5]

There will be no one to distribute the inheritance or to dispute over it, because all lose the inheritance; there is no need for disputes and courts and casting lots to divide the lands and fields, since everything passes into the hand of the seizing enemy. Their covetousness extends to everything: seizing fields, houses and inheritance, so that the peasants become destitute, with no shelter, deprived of the blessing of the inheritance of their fathers and forefathers.

God declares to the covetous that, since they unjustly rob the poor, what they have seized will be taken away from them, and they will even lose their money, so that they will have no portion in the land which God gave to His people.

entries.section: 3. Their rejection of the word of prophecy:

paragraphs.text: They prophesy, saying:
"Prophesy ye not."
They shall not prophesy concerning these things.
The disgrace shall not depart. [6]

After speaking of the sin of covetousness and the sins that followed it, such as the devising of evil, injustice, seizure and haughtiness, he speaks of a grave sin, which is resisting the word of the Lord, for they demand that the mouths of the prophets be shut. They do not stop at rebelling against civil laws, but rebel also against the authority of God. The wicked cannot endure the word of the Lord, nor do they accept rebuke, so they asked the prophet to keep silent and cease prophesying, counting the word of the Lord as disgrace and shame. They see in the word of the Lord a disturbance and terror to their souls. Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, sent to Jeroboam king of Israel asking him to prevent Amos from prophesying (Amos 7:10 ff.). And it is written in Isaiah: "Which say to the seers, See not" (Isa 30:10). This behavior remains even to the age of the Antichrist, when those who dwell on the earth are tormented by the preaching of the word (Rev 11:10).
We often reject frankness in the guidance of our life, and ask for soft words and deceptive human consolations, though we are in need of firmness springing from love.

entries.section: 4. The prophet does not keep silent:

paragraphs.text: 7 O thou that art named the house of Jacob, is the spirit of the LORD straitened? are these his doings? "do not my words do good to him that walketh uprightly? 8 Even of late my people is risen up as an enemy: ye pull off the robe with the garment from them that pass by securely as men averse from war. 9 The women of my people have ye cast out from their pleasant houses; from their children have ye taken away my glory for ever.
O thou that art named the house of Jacob, is the spirit of the LORD straitened?
Are these his doings?
Do not my words do good to him that walketh uprightly? [7]

He says: "O thou that art named the house of Jacob," for they bear the name but do not practice what befits their name. As the Apostle says: "Behold, thou art called a Jew, and restest in the law, and makest thy boast of God, and knowest his will, and approvest the things that are more excellent, being instructed out of the law; and art confident that thou thyself art a guide of the blind, a light of them which are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of babes, which hast the form of knowledge and of the truth in the law. Thou therefore which teachest another, teachest thou not thyself? thou that preachest a man should not steal, dost thou steal? thou that sayest a man should not commit adultery, dost thou commit adultery...?" (Rom 2:17-22).

The prophet did not keep silent as they asked him, but rebuked them, affirming to them that the secret of their disgrace is not his words but their conduct, which does not agree with the ways of the Lord, their life is not upright with the work of the Spirit of God. If it becomes upright, they receive the blessing of the Lord.

The prophet Micah rebukes them, saying: "Is the spirit of the LORD straitened?" meaning, do you think that you are able to silence the voice of the Lord and resist His Spirit? If you use every authority to silence the prophets, will the Spirit of God not find other ways to reprove you for your evil? Can your temporal authority and your material resources nullify the counsel of God?

And by his saying "Are these his doings?" he rebukes them, because they boast that they are the sons of Israel, the house of Jacob, and from them came the prophets. Did your father Jacob practice what you are doing? Do you walk in the same way as your father? You boast that you are the house of Jacob, but you do not do his works.

So also the Lord Christ rebuked the Jews when they boasted that they were the children of Abraham the free, while they wanted to kill the Lord Christ. Therefore He said to them: "If ye were Abraham's children, ye would do the works of Abraham. But now ye seek to kill me, a man that hath told you the truth, which I have heard of God: this did not Abraham. Ye do the deeds of your father... Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do" (Jn 8:39-44).
It is as though the prophet says to his people: You have the name "the house of Jacob," but your deeds testify that you are "the house of the devil, who resists the Spirit of the Lord."
If they wish to be ascribed to Jacob, who walked by the Spirit of the Lord, let them walk uprightly, as befits them.
St. Hippolytus of Rome sees that the house of Jacob provoked the wrath of God and was bound up with the sufferings of Christ according to the flesh.

* "And he was clothed with a vesture dipped in blood: and his name is called The Word of God" (Rev 19:13). See, then, my brethren, how the garment sprinkled with blood points to the flesh, through which the Word of God, who is not subject to suffering, endured suffering, as the prophet bears witness. For thus speaks the blessed Micah: "Must this be said, O house of Jacob? Is the spirit of the Lord short of patience? Are these his doings? Do not my words do good to him that walketh uprightly? But ye have risen up against my people as an enemy; ye strip the garment from the man of peace." This points to the sufferings of Christ in the flesh.
St. Hippolytus * Scripture is accustomed to call the priest an angel and a god, saying: "Thou shalt not revile the gods, nor curse the ruler of thy people." (Ex 22:28) LXX.

St. John Chrysostom * He who truly leaves this world and takes the yoke of Christ and learns from Him, and trains himself daily to bear toil, because the Lord is "meek and lowly in heart" (Mt 11:29), remains continually undisturbed by all trials, and for him "all things work together for good" (Rom 8:28). As the prophet (Micah) says, the words of God are good to him that walketh uprightly (Mic 2:7).
Abba Abraham Even of late my people is risen up as an enemy.

entries.section: 4. The prophet does not keep silent:

paragraphs.text: Ye pull off the robe with the garment from them that pass by securely as men averse from war. [8]

While they take pride in calling themselves "the house of Jacob" [7], they play the part of the enemy who shatters this house. They did not stand against the Spirit of the Lord only, but against the nation or the people as well, for in robbing the peasants they shatter "the house of Jacob," and are counted enemies resisting it. They are an internal enemy more dangerous than any external enemy.
The psalmist says: "For they speak not peace: but they devise deceitful matters against them that are quiet in the land" (Ps 35:20).
The hideousness of their conduct appears in that they not only rob the land, but even strip the robe from those who pass by securely, and from those whom they defended in battle.
The women of my people have ye cast out from their pleasant houses.

entries.section: 4. The prophet does not keep silent:

paragraphs.text: From their children have ye taken away my glory for ever. [9]

They devoured widows' houses (Mt 23:14), and took possession of them, and treated the women with a brutality inconsistent with humane conduct, especially since they were women of the same nation, women of the people of God, who seek God's protection for them.

Their hand stretched out to seize from the women their children to be slaves to them; perhaps they sold them as slaves to the pagan kingdoms, so that they deprived them of the enjoyment of faith in God, and stripped them of their glory.

Perhaps the prophet is pointing here to the captivity which God allowed because of the corruption and evil of the leaders, which spread among the people. For in captivity it does not stop at the seizing of women from their houses, but even the children lose their right to Hebrew nationality and to share in worship in the temple, as they are carried to a foreign land.

10 "Arise ye, and depart; for this is not your rest: because it is polluted, it shall destroy you, even with a sore destruction. 11 If a man walking in the spirit and falsehood do lie, saying, I will prophesy unto thee of wine and of strong drink; he shall even be the prophet of this people.
Arise ye, and depart; for this is not your rest.
Because it is polluted, it shall destroy you, even with a sore destruction. [10]

In bitterness he calls them to arise and depart into captivity, for the fruit of their uncleanness and the sore destruction has come upon them! The divine sentence of chastening has been pronounced upon them, for since they robbed the rights of the people by their temporal authority, their possessions are taken from them by force, and the Promised Land is no longer a place of rest for them.

There comes upon them what came upon their fathers who murmured against God in the wilderness again and again. As it is written in the Psalm: "Forty years long was I grieved with this generation, and said, It is a people that do err in their heart, and they have not known my ways: unto whom I sware in my wrath that they should not enter into my rest" (Ps 95:10-11).

It does not stop at their being driven out of the Promised Land, but "because it is polluted, it shall destroy you, even with a sore destruction": the secret of their destruction is not the military strength of the enemy who takes them captive, but their own destructive uncleanness. Therefore Scripture charges us: "having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust" (2 Pet 1:4), "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world" (Jas 1:27).
The prophet calls them to arise from the state of sin, so that they may enjoy true rest and destruction may not come upon them.

* Would that he who is unable to fly like the eagle might fly like a sparrow. He who is not able to fly to heaven, let him fly to those mountains. Would that he might fly before the valleys, these which are quickly destroyed by the waters. Let him cross over the mountains. The cousin of Abraham crossed over the mountains of Zoar (Segor) and was saved (Gen 19:12-29). But Lot's wife could not climb them, for she looked back in a womanly way and lost her salvation (Gen 19:26). The Lord says by the prophet Micah: "Draw near to the everlasting mountains, go up from here, for there is no rest for you in them because of uncleanness. By corruption ye are corrupted, ye suffer expulsion." He says: "Let them which be in Judaea flee into the mountains" (Mt 24:16). There is mount Zion, and so the city of peace Jerusalem, built not of earthly stones but of living stones, by an innumerable company of angels and the church of the firstborn and the spirits of just men made perfect, and by the God of the righteous who spoke by blood better than Abel (Heb 12:24). For one cried out for vengeance (Gen 14:10) and the other for forgiveness. One reproves his brother's sin, and the other forgives the sin of the world. One proclaims a crime and the other covers a crime, as it is written: "Blessed are they whose sins are covered" (Ps 32:1) LXX.

St. Ambrose * "In the Lord put I my trust: how say ye to my soul, Flee as a bird to your mountain?" (Ps 11:1) LXX. A violent enemy! He tempted the Lord the Savior in the wilderness, and now he seeks the believers, he seeks each one of them to leave the land of Judaea and dwell in a wilderness barren of virtues, so that he may crush them there very easily. Even the counsel itself (which he offers) is crafty. It is not an advice that (the believer) take the wings of a dove, the gentle, simple, tame bird, a bird of which they say that it has never any malice, the one which was offered in the temple for the Lord (Lk 2:24), but (he counsels them to take) the wings of a sparrow, a chattering (chirping), roving bird, which becomes a stranger to its mate after the young emerge from the eggs.
St. Jerome If a man walking in the spirit and falsehood do lie, saying:
I will prophesy unto thee of wine and of strong drink; he shall even be the prophet of this people! [11]

The prophet attacked their acceptance of the false prophets who, for the sake of their material or social benefit, overlook the truth and flatter the oppressors and cover up wrong. For this reason the Apostle says: "For if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10).

If someone came to speak to them of wine and strong drink, the oppressors would find in his talk what qualifies him to be a prophet to them, speaking to them of what they desire. They do not want a true prophet who utters the word of God, because for them it is disgrace and shame.

They want wicked prophets who agree with them in their evils, of whom it is said: "When thou sawest a thief, then thou consentedst with him, and hast been partaker with adulterers. Thou givest thy mouth to evil, and thy tongue frameth deceit" (Ps 50:18-19).

Perhaps he is pointing here to the false prophets who, instead of becoming drunk with the love of God and being occupied with the divine commandment, are occupied with the licentious feasts held by the rich, and fall into drunkenness, which robs them of their balance and turns them aside from their mission.
* No sooner had they begun to plunge into the abyss of excess and deviate from the natural senses than they surrendered their souls to captivity under the tyrant of corrupt drunkenness.

They resemble a ship without ballast to keep its balance, therefore it is said: [Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink] (cf. Isa 5:11). They do not satisfy a need, nor do they wait for the desire to subside, but this is their work, to be drunk continually. Therefore it is said: "that they may follow strong drink."
St. John Chrysostom

12 "I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as the flock in the midst of their fold: they shall make great noise by reason of the multitude of men. 13 The breaker is come up before them: they have broken up, and have passed through the gate, and are gone out by it: and their king shall pass before them, and the LORD on the head of them."

As is the habit of the prophets, after the threat of chastening and before its coming, they open the door of hope so that they may perceive the surpassing mercy of God. For when He chastens, it is in order to gather them to Himself, and to give them more than they ask and above what they seek.
I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee.
I will surely gather the remnant of Israel.
I will put them together as the sheep of the fold, as the flock in the midst of their fold: they shall make great noise by reason of the multitude of men. [12]

Some scholars see in these two statements [12-13] a prophecy of the return from captivity in the near future, and of the enjoyment of freedom from the captivity of sin by the coming of the Messiah, the Savior of the world.

A wonderful prophecy of two great events: the first, the return of Israel from the Babylonian captivity, and the second, the gathering together of the host of believers at the coming of the Lord Christ, who walks at their head as the firstborn from the dead and the heavenly head of the Church.

Others see that these two statements are the prophecy of the false, deceiving prophets that the captivity would end quickly and the return would be accomplished at once; this prophecy was not fulfilled.

If they were scattered because of their evil, then after chastening them He gathers them together, not as two divided kingdoms, but as one people and one kingdom, and calls all of them "Jacob." He will gather the holy remnant who clung to the Lord during the captivity and returned to Him, and they will become the sheep of His rational flock.

"They shall make great noise by reason of the multitude of men," or they make a commotion because of the great number, where the Lord Christ, the Good Shepherd, gathers His people from all nations: "that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad" (Jn 11:52). As He says: "And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd" (Jn 10:16).
The breaker is come up before them.
They have broken up, and have passed through the gate, and are gone out by it: and their king shall pass before them, and the LORD on the head of them. [13]

Who is this breaker who breaks through the gate and passes through it, and goes out and brings out his people with him, but the Lord Christ, who broke death; He put it to death by His death. He brought His people through the gate of Hades and entered with them into His Paradise, granting them the spirit of victory over the last enemy, which is death?

He became the firstborn from the dead and raised us with Him! He came out of the tomb and carried its gate, as Samson took the doors of the gate of the city and the two posts and pulled them up, bar and all, and put them upon his shoulders and went out (Judg 16:3).

Some see that the breaker here is St. John the Baptist, who came in the spirit of Elijah to prepare the way before the King of kings, the Savior of the world, for he opened the door by proclaiming repentance and calling to a meeting with the Lamb of God who bears the sin of the world.

In the midst of the darkness the Savior advances, the light of the world, to shine with His light and scatter the darkness. He is called here the breaker, that is, the remover of obstacles and the opener of the way toward eternity. He opens the door wide so that every believer may find in it hope to enter in and go out under His leadership.

* He who enters must not remain in the same state in which he entered, but must go to the pasture, so that the entering is the beginning of the perfection of graces: "shall go in and out, and find pasture" (Jn 10:9). He who enters is confined within the limits of the world, but he who continues to walk, as one passing beyond created things, reckoning what is seen as nothing, finds pasture above the heavens, and feeds on the word of God, saying: "The Lord is my shepherd (He feeds me); I shall not want" (Ps 23:1) LXX. But this entering cannot be accomplished except by Christ, as followed: "and the LORD on the head of them."
St. Jerome
Let Your Spirit work in me!

entries.section: 1. A call to the leaders to know the truth:

paragraphs.text: And I said, Hear, I pray you, O heads of Jacob, and ye princes of the house of Israel.
Is it not for you to know the truth? [1]
It was fitting for the elders of Israel to live in the midst of the people, sharing with them daily life, but they turned into a ruling aristocratic class living in the capital "Jerusalem."

And the judges, who ought to have taught the people the Law and borne witness to the divine truth, set the Law aside, and became more wicked than the people, with no work except the abuse of their positions and authority.

* Truly the prophets repeat the accusation against the people, saying: "Hear the word of the LORD, ye rulers of Sodom... thy princes are rebellious" (Isa 1:10, 23). Again Micah says: "Is it not for you to know justice?" In fact, everywhere they restrain them (discourage them) with violence. What, then? Does anyone ascribe the fault to God? Far be it from us to have this thought. For the fault is truly in them. For what virtuous excuse could anyone offer, that you do not know the law, other than that you refuse to obey it?

St. John Chrysostom * He addresses the leaders, who were entrusted with judgment and trampled justice; therefore he put this in the form of a question: Are you not those responsible for judgment, to punish the guilty and acquit the innocent without blame? How then did those who were entrusted with the administration of the laws turn aside from practicing good and zealously support evil? You have practiced such greed with regard to the needy, stripping them of all their possessions (he suggests this by saying: you have stripped the people of their skins and the body of its bones).

Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus We do not marvel if a simple prophet stood in a village to judge the heads and judges and to question them, for since he enjoys the divine truth he carries a special majesty, while these great men, since they did not know the truth in their life and conduct, became weak, unable to defend themselves.
Where the truth is, fear finds no place, but a man bears the fear of the Lord and in humility fears neither men nor events.

Who are those whom he questions: "Is it not for you to know the truth?" Truly they know it, and keep the Law and the statutes, perhaps by heart, but they are strangers to it in their life and conduct, and so became without knowledge.

2 Who hate the good, and love the evil; who pluck off their skin from off them, and their flesh from off their bones; 3 who also eat the flesh of my people, and flay their skin from off them; and they break their bones, and chop them in pieces, as for the pot, and as flesh within the caldron. 4 Then shall they cry unto the LORD, but he will not hear them: he will even hide his face from them at that time, as they have behaved themselves ill in their doings.
Who hate the good, and love the evil; who pluck off their skin from off them, and their flesh from off their bones. [2]
When the love of money and covetousness creep into the heart, a man loses his inner insight and discernment, and so hates good for others and desires evil for them.
The first mark of the oppressors is hatred of good and love of evil; they treat the poor as cannibals, holding their feasts by slaughtering the poor and cooking them.

In the Book of Ezekiel God rebukes the wicked shepherds, saying: "Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?... but with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them. And they were scattered, because there is no shepherd: and they became meat to all the beasts of the field, when they were scattered... Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against the shepherds; and I will require my flock at their hand, and cause them to cease from feeding the flock; neither shall the shepherds feed themselves any more; for I will deliver my flock from their mouth, that they may not be meat for them" (Ezek 34:2, 4, 10).
Who also eat the flesh of my people, and flay their skin from off them; and they break their bones, and chop them in pieces, as for the pot, and as flesh within the caldron. [3]
It was fitting for the spiritual leaders to give themselves for the sake of the people, not to satisfy their desires and prey upon the people like savage beasts, like eaters of human flesh.

He presents a hideous picture of the brutality that these leaders reached against the people, for they eat their flesh like beasts of prey, and flay their skins so as to leave no trace of their flesh, and break their bones to eat the marrow, and chop them in pieces as for the pot, as though they were cutting up their flesh and putting it in a pot! A most painful picture of their gluttony and their cruelty without limit!
Then shall they cry unto the LORD, but he will not hear them: he will even hide his face from them at that time, as they have behaved themselves ill in their doings. [4]

God will not hear the cries of him who eats his brother's flesh, however much they increase and however high they rise, but the Lord hides His face from them to let justice take its course at the appointed time. "For judgment is without mercy" (Jas 2:13). As they did not listen to the cries of their brothers when they were in ease and prosperity, they too cry out in their distress and find no answer. And as they hid their faces from their poor brothers, God hides His face from them. As Adoni-bezek said: "Threescore and ten kings, having their thumbs and their great toes cut off, gathered their meat under my table: as I have done, so God hath requited me" (Judg 1:7). And the psalmist says: "With the merciful thou wilt shew thyself merciful; with an upright man thou wilt shew thyself upright; with the pure thou wilt shew thyself pure; and with the froward thou wilt shew thyself froward. For thou wilt save the afflicted people; but wilt bring down high looks" (Ps 18:25-27). And Solomon the Wise says: "Whoso stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor, he also shall cry himself, but shall not be heard" (Prov 21:13).
* At the moment in which I withdraw from evil, at that very moment I become worthy that You listen to my prayers.

St. Jerome * You adapt the reward, O Lord, according to the directions of the people. You supply the saints with what holiness deserves, and the innocent and those free from sin with what befits them, and the chosen and the perfect with what is perfect; but as for those who turn aside from the straight way and walk in the opposite direction, You guarantee that they will find the end of their way, which befits them.
Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus

5 Thus saith the LORD concerning the prophets that make my people err, that bite with their teeth, and cry, Peace; and he that putteth not into their mouths, they even prepare war against him. 6 "Therefore night shall be unto you, that ye shall not have a vision; and it shall be dark unto you, that ye shall not divine; and the sun shall go down over the prophets, and the day shall be dark over them. 7 Then shall the seers be ashamed, and the diviners confounded: yea, they shall all cover their lips; for there is no answer of God."
Thus saith the LORD concerning the prophets that make my people err, that bite with their teeth, and cry, Peace!
And he that putteth not into their mouths, they even prepare war against him. [5]

While the false prophets bite the flesh of their brothers with their teeth like beasts of prey, they present honeyed, false words, proclaiming a false peace. These prophets are supported by the rich and those in authority, but it will not last, for war is surely coming!

Some translate "bite with their teeth" as "gnaw with their teeth"; for while they speak smooth things, proclaiming peace, they hide their lie by biting their lips with their teeth to hold back what is within them, so that no word escapes that would reveal their deceit and lying.

They are greedy, seeking to eat the flesh of others without ceasing. Their mouth is open to devour, and if anyone stops them they prepare war against him, threatening him with the harsh judgments of God. This is the work of covetousness for base gain (1 Tim 3:3; Titus 1:7).

* He (the prophet Jeremiah) says: "and all thy friends, to whom thou hast prophesied lies" (Jer 20:6). For he who speaks wickedly of the sayings of God, and casts the prophetic words into the pit, prophesies, but he prophesies lies.

* He did not forbid them merely from listening to a prophet, but they listen to the words of the prophets when they present vanity (Jer 23:16). For he who hears a prophet like Moses does not hear him but hears the Lord who speaks through him. For the false prophets work vanity. Since they speak visions that are from their own hearts, they do not change the heart of the hearer, and so they work vanity.
Origen Therefore night shall be unto you, that ye shall not have a vision.
It shall be dark unto you, that ye shall not divine.
And the sun shall go down over the prophets, and the day shall be dark over them. [6]

Since the false prophets ran after the love of money, they clung to the rich, walked in a spirit of hypocrisy, and justified injustice; so their minds became dark and their life turned into a night with no day, because they rejected the Sun of Righteousness. They lose all inner enlightenment, so their minds are darkened and their thoughts trouble them.

The Lord declares the helplessness of the false prophets, since they have no vision by night and no divination in the dark, and they come into a state of severe frustration, and shame and disgrace come upon them.

* "The sun shall go down" (Jer 15:9) on these prophets who lead my people astray, dwelling in darkness. "It shall be night to you, without vision, and it shall be darkness to you without dawn." For when (the unclean spirit) departs from a man, he passes through places (Mt 12:43). This happens exactly by nature. For (the Lord) returns this judgment upon the people. "Even so shall it be also unto this wicked generation" (Mt 12:45). For in the days of the prophets there went out from them (the unclean spirit) which is sin itself.
St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian Then shall the seers be ashamed, and the diviners confounded: yea, they shall all cover their lips; for there is no answer of God. [7]
If anyone asked the false prophets for counsel, they offered what was within them of darkness, because they have no "answer of God."
The covering of the lips also points to their inability to prophesy, so their tongue falls silent and they cover their lips, and the people grope their way in the midst of spiritual darkness.

By covering their upper lips is meant covering the mustache, since the Hebrew word is שָׂפָם (sapham). The mustache and beard had a special esteem among the Hebrews as a sign of courage, manliness and strength. So covering the upper lip is a sign of grief and sorrow. Thus the text here means that the prophets are in grief, because God refuses to reveal Himself to them, and for this reason they cover their lips. For this reason the leper is required to cover his upper lip (Lev 13:45). The same custom occurs in Ezekiel (Ezek 24:17, 22).

entries.section: 4. Micah and the power of the Spirit:

paragraphs.text: But truly I am full of power by the spirit of the LORD, and of truth and might, to declare unto Jacob his transgression, and to Israel his sin. [8]
While the false prophets will be exposed one day and put to shame, the prophet is vindicated continually through the work of the Spirit of the Almighty Lord and his holding fast to the divine truth.

Micah attributes the secret of his power to the work of the Holy Spirit in him. The Spirit of the Lord qualified him for the prophetic pastoral work, so he was filled with power, truth and courage, speaking as one who has authority. As Isaiah the prophet says: "For the Lord GOD will help me; therefore shall I not be confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be ashamed" (Isa 50:7). So he does not fear the opposition of men, even if they are men of authority!

The prophet realized his inability in himself to do this work, but the Spirit of the Lord is the secret of his power, because: "who is sufficient for these things?" (2 Cor 2:16), and as the Apostle says: "our sufficiency is of God" (2 Cor 3:5).

In contrast to the false prophets, upon whom severe frustration came, Micah was filled with the power of the divine Spirit, carrying inner strength, truth and might. He feels no weakness, nor does he lack knowledge of the truth, nor does he lose his heroic work in the Lord. It is as though he says to them: There is no basis for comparison between the false prophets and me, for "What is the chaff to the wheat?" (Jer 23:28).

Since the prophet Micah enjoyed these qualifications, he spoke boldly and declared to Jacob his transgression, and to Israel his sin. Men of God have sometimes been bound to reveal the sincerity of their mission and the divine abilities they enjoyed, not for boasting but for the sake of service and the building up of the Kingdom of God in this world.

In his interpretation of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians (2 Cor 11:21 ff.) St. John Chrysostom explains that the Apostle Paul did not do this in order to boast of himself, but to silence the mouths of those who wished to destroy his ministry by denying his apostleship. Chrysostom presented many examples of men of God who defended themselves for the building up of the Church and the success of the divine work. Samuel the prophet says: "Behold, here I am: witness against me before the LORD, and before his anointed: whose ox have I taken? or whose ass have I taken? or whom have I defrauded? whom have I oppressed? or of whose hand have I received any bribe to blind mine eyes therewith? and I will restore it you" (1 Sam 12:3). And Amos the prophet says to Amaziah: "I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: and the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel" (Amos 7:14 ff.), and so also the prophet Micah here.

9 Hear this, I pray you, ye heads of the house of Jacob, and princes of the house of Israel, that abhor the truth, and pervert all equity. 10 They build up Zion with blood, and Jerusalem with iniquity. 11 The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire, and the prophets thereof divine for money: yet will they lean upon the LORD, and say, Is not the LORD among us? none evil can come upon us. 12 Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of the forest.
Hear this, I pray you, ye heads of the house of Jacob, and princes of the house of Israel, that abhor the truth, and pervert all equity. [9]

Since the prophet Micah enjoys the Spirit of the Almighty Lord, he will not lack the ability to speak boldly against the heads and judges who hate the truth and pervert all that is straight. Perhaps by perverting all equity he means the misinterpretation of the word of the Lord, so that they turn it to their own private advantage. This is also what the heretics do when they misuse certain scriptural phrases in the service of their heresies.

In his letter [19:8] St. Cyril the Great wrote about those who corrupt the truth by misusing certain phrases from the Holy Bible. He also sent with the letter a copy of the letter of St. Athanasius the Apostolic to Epicetetus, which the heretics had distorted.
They build up Zion with blood, and Jerusalem with iniquity. [10]

The leaders of the nation sought to build a prosperous city, so they were occupied with magnificent constructions and outward appearances at the expense of the poor class of the people. They care for the appearance and beauty of the city like those who seek the public good, while they break the Law and oppress the poor.

* "They build up Zion with blood" (Mic 3:10). They did not learn self-control, though they received this commandment first: "Thou shalt not kill," and were commanded to refrain from countless other things because of this, and in many various ways they were urged to keep this commandment. Yet they did not stop this evil habit, but what did they say when they saw Him? Come, let us kill Him. And what was the motive? What was the reason? What accusation, great or small, did they bring against Him? Is it because He honors you, and because He, being God, became man for your sake, and wrought countless wonders? Or because He forgave your sins? Or because He called you to the Kingdom? That you may see their great evil with their folly, and the cause of killing Him is their utter madness.
St. John Chrysostom The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire, and the prophets thereof divine for money: yet will they lean upon the LORD, and say:
Is not the LORD among us?
None evil can come upon us! [11]

The prophet condemns the religious leaders who work as hirelings, whom the bribe seduces, and who turn aside because of the love of money. He also warns the rich and those in authority against using their resources to influence the servants of God; this is counted as a bribe! The false prophets turned into mercenaries who prophesy according to the silver offered to them, so they are occupied not with declaring the will of God but with how they may gain money. They imitated Balaam, who "loved the wages of unrighteousness" (2 Pet 2:15).

* You, O priest, are permitted to live from the altar, not to live in luxury. The mouth of the ox that treads out the corn is not muzzled. The Apostle did not abuse his liberty, but having food and raiment he was content, working night and day so as not to be chargeable to anyone (1 Thess 2:6; 2 Thess 3:8). And in his epistle he calls God to witness that he lived with dignity (1 Thess 2:10), without covetousness, in the gospel of Christ. He also affirmed, not concerning himself alone but concerning his disciples, that he sent no one to ask or take anything from the churches. But if in some epistles he expressed his pleasure and called the gifts which some sent the grace of God (2 Cor 12:17-18), he did not gather them for himself but for the poor saints of Jerusalem, who were the Jews who first believed in Christ, and whom their fathers and relatives drove out, and they lost their possessions and all their interests, which the priests of the temple and the people had ruined. Let these accept to take. But under the cover of the poor a few grew rich, and eat from vessels of gold and glass and china (precious porcelain). Would that by our wealth we might change our habit, or not allow the poor to be a cause for the attainment of wealth by the nobles...

St. Jerome All the civil and religious leaders, the heads, priests and prophets, agreed upon one thing, which is the love of money. And through their practice of worship in its formality without spirit they thought that God was in their midst protecting them from every evil. They think that these evil acts of theirs cause no harm, because they are the people of God in name.
